body:
## Module 1 in two minutes

**A task audit lists things to automate. A decision audit lists things somebody has to be able to defend.** Only the second one survives an auditor, a works council, or a lawyer, and in a systems role, the risk sits almost entirely in decisions that were made once, encoded, and then abandoned while still executing.

Somebody decided that leave requests over ten days route to a second approver. It runs four hundred times a year. Nobody knows who decided it or why. **That is a decision wearing a process step's clothes**, and your stack is full of them, eligibility rules, approval thresholds, picklist definitions, the tolerance at which a payroll variance triggers a hold.

The diagnostic question is short: **can you name the person (not the team) who would defend this if it were challenged?** If you can't, it is a deferred decision. And it matters for one practical reason: you can't enable AI on a decision nobody owns, because there is nobody to sign the enablement.

So AI on top of an unowned decision doesn't create an accountability gap. **It inherits one that was already there and makes it move faster.**

### You are not behind, and you didn't decide

HR technology management is the **second-highest AI adoption area in HR at around 21%**, behind only recruiting's 27%, inside a function where **54% of organizations have deployed no AI in HR at all and have no plans to this year**, while 92% of CHROs expect more of it anyway. You're the front line of a function that mostly hasn't started.

But almost none of it was your decision, because AI arrives through three doors and only one has a gate. **A feature in a system you already own**: a release note, no review, largest volume by far. **A new product** — procurement, security review, signature: the only gated door, and where all the governance attention sits. **Employees using their own tools**, invisible.

The evidence door one is real: nearly **one-third of organizations do not know whether AI features exist in their current HR systems** (Sapient Insights, 9,886 professionals across 4,670 organizations). Your function is counted as second-most-adopted while a third of organizations can't say what is in their own estate. Both findings are sound. **The space between them is door one.**

**The full module builds the register**, six columns per decision: volume, reach, detection latency, reversibility, accountability *by name*, and defensibility. Blanks are entries, not failures; a register with no gaps is almost always one somebody guessed at. Twelve real rows beat forty plausible ones.

Two of those columns carry the track. Plot decisions on **reach** against **detection latency**, and the quadrant that matters is wide reach with long latency: everyone affected, nobody notices for a month. **It is also exactly where AI is sold to you**: bulk data operations, automated transactions, agentic workflows, mass communications. Not because vendors are careless, but because the labour savings and the blast radius have the same cause.

Which changes two things you inherited from 201. **Size verification to latency, not just stakes** — the same error rate costs a nuisance if caught today and a year of transactions if caught at the audit. And **reversibility is the gate, not accuracy**: accuracy you measure afterwards, reversibility you design beforehand. An effective-dated bulk change that already reached payroll and the carriers isn't an undo, it is a correction project.

And for anything with a statutory clock under it: I-9, COBRA, ACA furnishing, final pay: **AI can prepare and remind. It cannot be the control.** A control has to produce evidence it ran, and a reminder nobody acknowledged is a log entry that gets read out loud to you later.
